prompt: By the definition this lesson uses, which of these is an architectural decision?
hint: Ask what it would cost to reverse a year from now.

choices.text: Renaming `orders_place` to `place_order` across the whole program
choices.why: A rename takes a minute with an editor; nothing else depends on the old name for long.

choices.text: Keeping every module's tables in one shared database
choices.why: Right. Other code, other teams and real data come to depend on it, so undoing it takes weeks.

choices.text: Choosing a colour for the shop's buttons and the logo on every page
choices.why: Cheap to change at any time, and nothing else is built on it.

choices.text: Adding a comment above `stock_take`
choices.why: A comment changes no behaviour and costs nothing to remove.

prompt: Match each quality attribute to the question it asks.
hint: The table in the first section.

pairs.right: What share of the time does it answer?
How long does one request take?
How many requests can it take per second?
How many people must agree to a change?

right_distractors: How many lines of code does it have?

prompt: A team replicates its database to a second region so that the shop keeps answering when the first region goes down. Which attribute is it most likely to pay with?
hint: Two copies of the data, written at two moments.

choices.text: Modifiability
choices.why: Replication does not make the code harder to change.

choices.text: Throughput
choices.why: A replica adds capacity for reads rather than taking it away.

choices.text: Consistency
choices.why: Right. Two copies can disagree for a while, which is lessons 8 and 9.

choices.text: Availability
choices.why: That is what it buys, not what it pays with.

prompt: Which path does the lesson recommend for the machine the course is done on?
hint: The same shape as the one the transcripts came from.

choices.text: A Codespace in the browser
choices.why: Named so that you know it exists; its free hours are somebody else's decision.

choices.text: An Ubuntu VM made with Multipass, with Docker Engine inside
choices.why: Right: same shape as the lab, and free to throw away.

choices.text: Docker Engine installed straight on the computer you use every day, with no VM
choices.why: It works, and leaves every container of the course on your everyday machine.

choices.text: A server rented from a cloud provider
choices.why: Not one of the three paths, and it costs money from the first hour.

prompt: How many gigabytes of memory does the lesson ask for the course's virtual machine?
hint: The `--memory` flag of `multipass launch`.

prompt: You ran `sudo usermod -aG docker $USER` and `docker ps` still says permission denied. What is missing?
hint: When does a new group membership reach your shell?

choices.text: Restarting the Docker daemon
choices.why: The daemon is running and answered; it is your shell that has the old groups.

choices.text: Running `sudo chmod 666 /var/run/docker.sock`
choices.why: That gives every account on the machine root, by another route.

choices.text: Logging out and in again
choices.why: Right. The group is read at login, so `exit` and `multipass shell arch` again.

choices.text: Reinstalling the `docker-ce` package
choices.why: The package is fine; reinstalling does not change your session's groups.

prompt: A container exits with code 137 and `docker inspect` says `"OOMKilled": false`. What ran out?
hint: 137 is 128 plus 9. Whose limit was it, if not the container's?

choices.text: The memory of the VM itself
choices.why: Right. The kernel killed the process for the whole machine, not for the container's own limit.

choices.text: The disk
choices.why: A full disk gives `no space left on device`, not a kill signal.

choices.text: The container's own memory limit
choices.why: Then `OOMKilled` would say `true`, as it did in the transcript.

choices.text: Docker Hub's pull limit
choices.why: That fails before the container starts, with a 429.

prompt: `docker compose up` ends with `Bind for 127.0.0.1:8000 failed: port is already allocated`. What does that tell you?
hint: Who else wants that port?

choices.text: The image failed to build
choices.why: The containers were created; the build had already finished.

choices.text: Port 8000 is reserved by the operating system
choices.why: Nothing reserves 8000; something running is holding it.

choices.text: Something already running holds the port
choices.why: Right, often a container from an earlier lesson. `docker ps` names it and `docker compose down` in its directory frees it.

choices.text: The firewall in front of the VM blocked the connection
choices.why: Nothing has connected yet; this is the container failing to listen.

prompt: `apt-get` cannot get its lock a minute after the VM booted. What should you do?
hint: Who else installs packages right after a boot?

choices.text: Delete the lock file under `/var/lib/dpkg` and run the command again
choices.why: That is how a package database gets corrupted.

choices.text: Wait a few minutes for Ubuntu's own updates, then run it again
choices.why: Right. Only one program may install at a time.

choices.text: Reboot the VM in a loop until it works
choices.why: Each boot starts the same updates again.

choices.text: Make a new VM with more memory
choices.why: The lock is about a second installer running, not about memory.

prompt: Why does the shop store a price of R$ 32,90 as `3290`?
hint: What does `0.1 + 0.2` give in a floating-point number?

choices.text: To save space in the database
choices.why: Both forms are a few bytes; space is not the reason.

choices.text: Because SQLite has no decimal type at all to hold it
choices.why: The choice would be the same in a database that has one.

choices.text: Integers are exact; binary floating point is not
choices.why: Right. Binary floating point cannot represent most decimal fractions, and integer cents add up to the cent.

choices.text: To hide the real prices from anybody reading the browser's traffic
choices.why: Anybody can read `3290` and divide by a hundred.

prompt: Two bags of coffee at `3290` cents each were ordered. What `total_cents` did the shop answer?
hint: Price times quantity.

prompt: In the shop as written, how many processes answer a request that lists the products, and one that places an order?
hint: `docker compose ps` showed one container running one command.

choices.text: One for the catalogue and four for the order, one per module
choices.why: Modules are parts of the program, not processes of their own.

choices.text: The same single process for both
choices.why: Right. Every module is a function call inside `python app.py`.

choices.text: Two: one for reads and one for writes
choices.why: Nothing in the shop separates reads from writes; lesson 13 does.

choices.text: One per request, started on demand
choices.why: The server is started once and handles requests on threads.

prompt: The compose file publishes the shop on `127.0.0.1:8000`, so it can be reached only from the machine's own ___.
hint: The interface whose address starts with 127.

prompt: A card ending in `0002` is declined after the order row was inserted and the coffee was taken. What does the shop's data look like afterwards?
hint: Everything happened inside `with con:`.

choices.text: The order exists with no payment, and the coffee is gone
choices.why: That would be the state without a transaction around the three changes.

choices.text: The order row is gone, and the two bags of coffee stay taken out of stock
choices.why: The rollback undoes every change in the block, the stock included.

choices.text: As if nothing had happened: no order, no payment, the same stock
choices.why: Right. The exception rolled back all three changes.

choices.text: It depends on how long the charge took
choices.why: Timing does not decide it; the transaction does.

prompt: Coffee started with 12 units, an order for 2 was paid, a second for 1 was declined, and a third for 50 was refused. How many units does the catalogue show?
hint: Only one of the three changed anything.

prompt: What makes the shop refuse an order for 50 bags of coffee when it has 10?
hint: Look at the stock table's definition.

choices.text: A check in `orders_place` that compares the quantity with the stock
choices.why: There is no such comparison in the code; the database does it.

choices.text: The `CHECK (units >= 0)` on the stock table
choices.why: Right. It refuses the update, the transaction rolls back, and the `IntegrityError` becomes the 409.

choices.text: The payment module, which declines large amounts
choices.why: It declines one card suffix, whatever the amount.

choices.text: The catalogue, which hides products that run out
choices.why: The catalogue only lists; it never refuses an order.

prompt: Quitanda moves payments into its own service with its own database. What happens to the guarantee `with con:` gave?
hint: Can one database's transaction reach into another's?

choices.text: It still holds, because both services commit at the same moment
choices.why: Two commits at the same moment are still two commits; either can fail alone.

choices.text: It still holds as long as the network is fast
choices.why: Speed does not make two databases one.

choices.text: It no longer covers the payment
choices.why: Right. The shop needs another way to undo a half-finished order, and lesson 14 is that way, the saga.

choices.text: It holds for the payment and is lost for the stock
choices.why: Neither side is special; the boundary is the database.

prompt: What is a modular monolith?
hint: How many deploys, and what rule inside?

choices.text: One deployable program, split into modules that own their data
choices.why: Right. One deploy, and modules that meet only through public functions.

choices.text: Several small services that all read and write one shared database
choices.why: That is a distributed monolith, which lesson 2 warns about.

choices.text: A monolith with every module in a separate container
choices.why: Separate containers would make them services.

choices.text: A monolith whose code is in several repositories
choices.why: Repositories are about storage of the code, not boundaries at run time.

prompt: Which line of Quitanda's `app.py` breaks the modular rule the lesson describes?
hint: Which module reads a table it does not own?

choices.text: `stock_take` updating `stock`
choices.why: The stock module writing its own table is exactly the rule.

choices.text: `catalogue_list` joining `products` with `stock`
choices.why: Right. The catalogue reads the stock module's table instead of asking it.

choices.text: `payments_charge` inserting into `payments`
choices.why: That is the payments module's own table.

choices.text: `orders_place` calling `stock_take`
choices.why: Calling another module's public function is the allowed route.

prompt: Match each tool to how it enforces module boundaries.
hint: Each language has its own.

pairs.right: a Python check that fails on forbidden imports
tests in Java that assert which packages may depend on which
the toolchain refuses an import from outside the parent directory
a Ruby tool that checks dependencies between packages

right_distractors: a load balancer that routes requests per module

prompt: A team wants to split a big ball of mud into services next quarter. What does the lesson suggest as the first step?
hint: Where is it cheaper to move a boundary?

choices.text: Put each folder of the code in its own container straight away
choices.why: The folders of a ball of mud are not boundaries; the services would call each other's tables over a network.

choices.text: Rewrite the whole system from scratch as services, beside the old one
choices.why: Lesson 15 explains why big rewrites tend to fail.

choices.text: Turn it into modules that own their data, inside the one program
choices.why: Right. A module with its own data and a public surface is a service waiting for a network.

choices.text: Add a second database and let each team choose which to use
choices.why: Two shared databases are two balls of mud.

prompt: A team of six is building a new product whose idea of an order changes every few weeks. What does the lesson recommend?
hint: MonolithFirst, and why.

choices.text: A monolith, divided into modules, until the boundaries stop moving
choices.why: Right. A split along the wrong line costs more than no split.

choices.text: One service per entity from the first day, to be ready for growth
choices.why: Each change of idea would then be a change to several APIs.

choices.text: Serverless functions, one per endpoint
choices.why: That multiplies the boundaries rather than waiting for them.

choices.text: Two services, one for reads and one for writes
choices.why: That is CQRS, lesson 13, a different force.

prompt: What is the microservice premium Martin Fowler named in 2015?
hint: Paid before any benefit arrives.

choices.text: The licence fee charged by the vendors of service mesh products
choices.why: It is not a price list; the mesh is lesson 3.

choices.text: The extra speed a system gains by splitting
choices.why: Splitting adds latency rather than speed.

choices.text: The fixed cost of running a system as services
choices.why: Right: deployment, monitoring and failure handling, paid before any benefit. Below some complexity it is never earned back.

choices.text: The salary difference between backend and platform engineers
choices.why: Nothing in the idea is about salaries.

prompt: Which of these are reasons the lesson gives for keeping a monolith? Choose all that apply.
hint: Four of them are in the section.

choices.text: One team works on it
choices.why: Right: nobody to coordinate deploys with.

choices.text: Atomic transactions across all the data
choices.why: Right: four changes or none.

choices.text: Each module can use a different language
choices.why: That is a reason to split, not to keep.

choices.text: Function calls instead of network calls
choices.why: Right: nanoseconds instead of milliseconds.

choices.text: One thing to deploy, monitor and debug
choices.why: Right: operations stay small.

prompt: The catalogue gets a thousand times the traffic of the rest of Quitanda. What happens if the shop is scaled as it is?
hint: What does each copy contain?

choices.text: Only the catalogue is copied, because it is the only busy module
choices.why: A monolith cannot copy part of itself.

choices.text: Every copy carries all four modules, three of them idle
choices.why: Right. It works, and it pays for what is not busy.

choices.text: It cannot be scaled at all while it is a monolith
choices.why: More copies behind a load balancer work, and are often the cheapest answer.

choices.text: The database is copied with it, one per container
choices.why: The copies share one database; the figure has one load balancer and three program copies.

prompt: Five teams share one monolith and complain that their releases wait for each other. Which first step does the lesson's table point to?
hint: The right-hand column, for that force.

choices.text: Splitting every module into its own service in one go, next quarter
choices.why: The table points at the cheaper step first, and a split of one module when that is not enough.

choices.text: Adding a cache in front of the busiest module so that it answers faster
choices.why: That answers uneven load, not teams blocking each other.

choices.text: Adding bulkheads inside the process, one pool of threads per team
choices.why: Those fence a fault in; they do not change how releases work.

choices.text: A modular monolith with owners per module and a faster pipeline
choices.why: Right. That attacks the release train without paying the premium yet.

prompt: In a single process, what happens to the checkout when the report module leaks memory until the process is killed?
hint: How many processes are there?

choices.text: It keeps working, because the checkout lives in another module of the code
choices.why: Modules share the process; when it dies, all of them do.

choices.text: It goes down with the report, because they share the process
choices.why: Right. A fault anywhere is a fault everywhere.

choices.text: It slows down but stays up
choices.why: A killed process answers nothing at all.

choices.text: Docker restarts only the report module and leaves the checkout running
choices.why: Docker restarts containers, and the whole program is one container.

prompt: Put these responses to a growing monolith in the order the lesson suggests trying them, cheapest first.
hint: The table's right-hand column comes before any split.
trap: Splitting before naming a force is the fashion the lesson warns about.
items: Try the step that keeps the monolith
Move one module out, for that one reason
Pay for the split's operations from its first day

prompt: Quitanda's payments module needs a library that only runs on a newer runtime than the rest of the program can use. Which response fits best?
hint: A force that asks for running one module apart.

choices.text: Upgrade every module's runtime in one release, so that they all match
choices.why: Possible, and it makes every team pay for one module's need at once.

choices.text: Split the whole monolith into services
choices.why: The force names one module; the split should be that small.

choices.text: Move the payments module out as its own service, and only that one
choices.why: Right. One module, moved for one named reason.

choices.text: Run more copies of the monolith
choices.why: More copies do not change which runtime each one has.

prompt: Somebody says the monolith must be split because "serious systems use microservices". What is missing from the argument?
hint: The skill the last section names.

choices.text: The cost of the cloud bill after the split
choices.why: Cost is one force among several; the gap is that none is named.

choices.text: A force: which problem the split solves
choices.why: Right. With no force named it is a fashion.

choices.text: A diagram of the target architecture, signed off by the team
choices.why: A diagram writes a decision down; it does not justify it.

choices.text: The name of the framework the services would be written in
choices.why: Choosing tools comes after deciding there is a reason to split.

prompt: Match each force on a monolith to the cheaper first step the lesson gives for it.
hint: The table at the end of the last section.

pairs.right: module owners and a faster pipeline

pairs.left: one module with very different load
pairs.right: more copies, with a cache before the hot part

pairs.left: a fault in one part taking down the rest
pairs.right: timeouts and bulkheads in the process

prompt: Which of these would a split into services take away from Quitanda, and nothing else in the list would?
hint: The section about four changes or none.

choices.text: The ability to run more copies of the shop
choices.why: Services can run more copies too, one service at a time.

choices.text: The ability to publish the shop on a port
choices.why: Every service publishes a port of its own.

choices.text: The ability to keep prices in cents
choices.why: A representation of money survives any split.

choices.text: One transaction covering the order, the stock and the payment
choices.why: Right. With two databases no `with con:` reaches both.
